periods.analysis: 2024-Q3 establishes a solid green baseline for Rapid Emergency Response: Priority-1 response time was 6.2 minutes against the <= 7 target, officer training reached 346 hours against the >= 320 target, and 911 call abandonment was 4.3% against the <= 5 target. With no prior quarter in this series, the important fact is that all three controls cleared standard during the late-summer waterfront load, including Harborfest weekends and heavier traffic on Seawall Avenue. The joint CAD/AVL review showed the strongest gains on Beats 2 and 4 after we held two cars at the North Pier post during peak call windows. This is the kind of green result we can trust because it is supported by staffing discipline, not luck.
periods.recommendations: Keep the North Pier peak-posting plan in place through the next special-event cycle and document it as Standard Operating Procedure RE-24-3. Extend the dispatcher callback script pilot from the B-shift console to all shifts so the 4.3% abandonment rate remains below target. Continue scheduling scenario blocks in four-hour increments to protect the training margin above 320 hours without pulling too many officers off patrol at once.

periods.analysis: Performance strengthened in 2024-Q4, with Priority-1 response time improving from 6.2 to 5.9 minutes, officer training hours increasing from 346 to 355, and 911 abandonment falling from 4.3% to 3.5%. The green status is supported by the holiday deployment plan: traffic officers pre-cleared the Lighthouse Market corridor, and dispatch used the new Queue Watch board during parade and shopping peaks. The 0.3-minute response improvement is meaningful because it came during darker commuting hours and wet-road conditions, when small delays usually accumulate. Community trust benefits when residents see that the same procedure works under seasonal pressure.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Queue Watch board as a permanent dispatch supervisor check every 30 minutes during high-volume periods. Carry forward the Lighthouse Market traffic-control map for future events and add the ferry-terminal detour points before spring tourism begins. Use the 355 training hours to identify which modules produced the fastest field adoption, then repeat those modules first in Q1.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q1, the objective remained green even as Priority-1 response time moved up from 5.9 to 6.2 minutes and 911 abandonment edged up from 3.5% to 3.8%. Officer training hours rose sharply from 355 to 404, giving supervisors a wider skills base for de-escalation, first-arriving medical aid, and coastal-storm incident command. The slight response-time and abandonment increases are within standard, and they align with January storm watches and several bridge-lane closures near Harborview High. The procedural takeaway is clear: the system absorbed winter friction without breaching the public promise of <= 7 minutes and <= 5%.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the Q1 training cadence, but cap academy pull-outs on Fridays so the 404-hour effort does not reduce field coverage during weekend call surges. Pre-stage one patrol unit south of the bridge when Public Works posts lane restrictions, using CAD event tag BR-17 for tracking. Have dispatch supervisors review the 3.8% abandonment intervals by hour of day and adjust lunch relief coverage before the spring volume rises.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q2 stayed green, though all three measures showed pressure: Priority-1 response time moved from 6.2 to 6.3 minutes, officer training hours decreased from 404 to 387, and 911 abandonment rose from 3.8% to 4.5%. These values remain within target, but the quarter reflected real operating strain from beach traffic, two marina construction detours, and heavier Saturday calls along Route 6. The reduced training total is still well above the >= 320 standard, and the higher abandonment rate did not cross the <= 5 threshold. This is a watchful green: acceptable, but not a reason to relax procedure.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Route 6 beach-traffic unit active on Saturdays and add a second flex car from 1400 to 1800 during heat advisories. Protect at least 360 officer training hours next quarter by moving firearms requalification to split squads rather than full-shift blocks. For 911, open the seasonal call-taker overtime list two weeks earlier and monitor abandonment daily if it exceeds 4.2% for three consecutive days.

periods.analysis: The Q2 pressure eased in 2025-Q3 while the objective remained green: Priority-1 response time improved from 6.3 to 6.2 minutes, training hours declined from 387 to 347, and 911 abandonment improved from 4.5% to 4.2%. The lower abandonment rate reflects the seasonal staffing roster at the Harborview Communications Center and better triage of non-emergency beach-noise calls to the online HView311 form. Training hours are still above the >= 320 target, but the quarter-over-quarter decline is worth managing because we are using that training to protect consistency across a growing city. The response-time improvement confirms that the Beach Route patrol and Marina Lot staging plan are working as designed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Beach Route patrol through the first two weeks of the school year, then convert it to a Friday-Saturday surge assignment if call maps support it. Rebuild the training buffer by scheduling two 12-officer cohorts for scenario-based Priority-1 arrival drills in October. Keep HView311 messaging on beach-noise and parking complaints so emergency lines stay available for true Priority-1 calls.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q4 delivered another green quarter and moved the trend in the right direction: Priority-1 response time improved from 6.2 to 6 minutes, officer training increased from 347 to 360 hours, and 911 abandonment fell from 4.2% to 3.6%. The winter readiness package helped, including CAD geofencing for the Old Harbor district and pre-assigned units for school dismissal around Bayside Elementary. The 0.6-point drop in abandonment is especially important because it shows dispatch discipline improved after the summer surge rather than merely benefiting from lower volume. This is measured progress, and it reinforces the trust residents place in the first call for help.
periods.recommendations: Adopt the Old Harbor CAD geofence as a standing winter tool and add quarterly validation of boundary accuracy by the GIS analyst and watch commanders. Maintain the 360-hour training level as the minimum planning assumption for Q1, with priority on cold-weather crash response and domestic-violence call coordination. Continue the dispatch relief schedule that supported the 3.6% abandonment rate, and audit five randomly selected Priority-1 calls per week for call-processing time.

periods.analysis: In 2026-Q1, Rapid Emergency Response remained green with Priority-1 response time moving from 6 to 6.2 minutes, officer training hours increasing from 360 to 422, and 911 abandonment edging from 3.6% to 3.7%. The 422 training hours are the strongest result in this series so far and reflect the new Harborview Response Academy blocks for active-threat response, crisis communication, and coordinated fire-police staging. The small response-time increase is acceptable and expected during the winter academy cycle, provided supervisors continue to protect minimum beat coverage. The abandonment rate remained stable, which tells me the communications floor handled the training and backfill plan responsibly.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Harborview Response Academy, but publish a beat-coverage floor for each training day so the 6.2-minute response time does not drift upward. Convert the best academy scenarios into 20-minute roll-call refreshers for officers who were not in the 2026-Q1 cohorts. Sustain dispatch stability by retaining the current relief call-taker pool and cross-training two additional records clerks for emergency overflow support.

periods.analysis: 2026-Q2 stayed green, but it shows the operating pressure of a fast-growing coastal city: Priority-1 response time moved from 6.2 to 6.4 minutes, officer training hours decreased from 422 to 399, and 911 abandonment rose from 3.7% to 4.5%. All three measures still meet target, and 399 training hours remains a strong cushion above the >= 320 requirement. The response-time and abandonment movement aligns with early heat events, marina festival traffic, and construction around the Eastgate interchange, where units lost time entering Beats 5 and 6. This is not a failure; it is a clear instruction to tighten the summer operating plan before the margin gets thinner.
periods.recommendations: Activate the Summer Priority-1 Surge Plan by placing one flex unit at Eastgate from 1500 to 2100 and one downtown bicycle officer team on marina-event weekends. Hold training near 390 to 400 hours next quarter by shifting classroom modules to online prework and reserving in-person time for tactical skills. Treat 4.5% abandonment as the watch line: if any week exceeds it, add two four-hour call-taker shifts and route low-acuity reports to HView311 within the first recorded message.

periods.analysis: Training remains above standard, but 911 abandonment reached 5.3% against a 5.0% ceiling. Fire Station 7 improvement is 55% complete, with response-time analysis, coverage modeling, signal design and dispatch protocol revision still incomplete after their original deadlines. A resourced peak-hour squad pilot could address coverage sooner; signal preemption and dispatch coordination offer a longer-term option, but unfinished design and protocol testing prevent either from being counted as an achieved response-time gain. The response-time measure is left unchanged in this refresh.
periods.recommendations: Sam Okafor should confirm recovery dates for the late Station 7 work and arrange a dispatch exercise on November 12, 2026. Record staffing and call-routing issues, review the results before the revised November 20 protocol deadline, and compare pilot staffing needs with the signal installation schedule before deciding on deployment.
